slides.body: Five mistakes to watch for.

items: Taking a clean git status to mean "the directory equals the commit". Root cause: ignored files are present and hidden; git status --ignored lists them.
Thinking "tracked" means "committed". Root cause: tracked means "has an index entry"; a path becomes tracked at git add.
Reading a path listed twice as a contradiction. Root cause: status makes two comparisons, and a file staged and then edited again differs in both.
Parsing the long or short format in a script. Root cause: those formats follow user configuration and may change; --porcelain is the stable one, with -z for unusual file names.
Using git diff --exit-code to prove that a build left the tree clean. Root cause: it performs comparison two only, so a generator that created a new, untracked file passes unnoticed.

beats.text: A laptop build and a CI build of the same commit behave differently. CI is the automated system that builds and tests every change. The commit ID is identical. And somebody says "but git status is clean on my machine".
beats.tele: A laptop build and a CI build of the same commit behave differently. CI is the automated system that builds and tests every change. The commit ID is identical. And somebody says "but `git status` is clean on my machine".

beats.text: A clean git status doesn't mean the directory equals the commit. Ignored files, the ones Git has been told not to list, are present and invisible: a local .env file of settings, compiled caches, a stale build/ folder. Any tool that reads the directory sees the working tree, not the commit: a container build that copies the project directory, a packaging step, a test runner, an evaluation script.

Any tool that reads the directory sees the working tree, not the commit: a container build that copies the project directory, a packaging step, a test runner, an evaluation script.

beats.text: Hold on to one idea through all four. A version of a file can live in three places: in the working tree, in the index, or in a commit. The index is Git's list of what the next commit will contain. The working tree is the only one of the three with no history and no second copy. Git can rebuild tracked files in it from the index or from a commit. It can't rebuild content that never left it, such as an edit you haven't staged.

beats.text: Now precisely. The glossary defines the working tree as "the tree of actual checked out files", which "normally contains the contents of the HEAD commit's tree, plus any local changes that you have made but not yet committed". It starts at the directory that contains the dot git folder, called the top level, and every path Git prints is relative to that directory unless a command says otherwise.

beats.text: A repository can have no working tree, which is a bare repository, the form used on servers. Or one, the normal case. Or several, which are linked worktrees and belong to a later chapter.

beats.text: And inside the dot git folder? Nothing. The working tree isn't stored there at all. The only trace of it is in the index file. For each tracked path, the index remembers which blob the file last matched, and the file's size and timestamps, so that Git can find changed files without reading every file.

beats.text: Three categories. In one sentence: every path in the working tree is in exactly one of three categories, and the index decides which. Tracked, if it has an index entry. Ignored, if it has none and matches an ignore pattern. Untracked otherwise.
beats.tele: Three categories. In one sentence: every path in the working tree is in exactly one of three categories, and the index decides which. Tracked, if it has an index entry. Ignored, if it has none and matches an ignore pattern. Untracked otherwise.

beats.text: A tracked path is shown by git status when it differs from the index or from HEAD. git ls-files lists it. git add . updates it. git clean never touches it.
beats.tele: A tracked path is shown by `git status` when it differs from the index or from HEAD. `git ls-files` lists it. `git add .` updates it. `git clean` never touches it.

beats.text: An untracked path is shown under "Untracked files". git add . adds it. git clean removes it.
beats.tele: An untracked path is shown under "Untracked files". `git add .` adds it. `git clean` removes it.

beats.text: An ignored path is hidden unless you pass --ignored. git add . does not add it, unless you force it with -f. git clean removes it only with -x or -X.
beats.tele: An ignored path is hidden unless you pass `--ignored`. `git add .` does not add it, unless you force it with `-f`. `git clean` removes it only with `-x` or `-X`.

beats.text: Two consequences follow from the definitions. "Ignored" is a kind of untracked, so a tracked path can never be ignored. And "tracked" says nothing about commits: a path becomes tracked the moment git add writes its index entry. Almost everyone hears "tracked" as "committed" at first. It means: has an index entry.

beats.text: The anatomy of git status. In one sentence: git status is two comparisons and one scan. HEAD against the index. The index against the working tree. And a scan of the working tree for paths that have no index entry.
beats.tele: The anatomy of `git status`. In one sentence: `git status` is two comparisons and one scan. HEAD against the index. The index against the working tree. And a scan of the working tree for paths that have no index entry.

beats.text: The manual describes the same three parts. The first is what git commit would record. The second and third are what you could still add.
beats.tele: The manual describes the same three parts. The first is what `git commit` would record. The second and third are what you could still add.

beats.text: The short format puts the two comparisons in two columns. The first column, X, is comparison one: HEAD against the index. The second column, Y, is comparison two: the index against the working tree.
beats.tele: The short format puts the two comparisons in two columns. The first column, X, is comparison one: HEAD against the index. The second column, Y, is comparison two: the index against the working tree.

beats.text: M and a space: a modification is staged, and the working tree matches the index. A space and M: modified in the working tree, not staged. MM: staged, then modified again. A and a space: a new file is staged. D and a space: a deletion is staged. A space and D: the file was deleted in the working tree, and the deletion is not staged. R and a space: a rename is staged. Two question marks: untracked. Two exclamation marks: ignored, shown only with --ignored.
beats.tele: `M` and a space: a modification is staged, and the working tree matches the index. A space and `M`: modified in the working tree, not staged. `MM`: staged, then modified again. `A` and a space: a new file is staged. `D` and a space: a deletion is staged. A space and `D`: the file was deleted in the working tree, and the deletion is not staged. `R` and a space: a rename is staged. Two question marks: untracked. Two exclamation marks: ignored, shown only with `--ignored`.

beats.text: Formats for scripts. There are two stable formats. --porcelain, version 1, looks like the short format, but it's guaranteed not to change between Git versions or with user configuration, and it always prints paths relative to the top level. --porcelain=v2 adds the file modes and object IDs that status compared. Add -z when file names may contain spaces or newlines: entries are then separated by NUL bytes and never quoted.

Add `-z` when file names may contain spaces or newlines: entries are then separated by NUL bytes and never quoted.

beats.text: Three details that matter in practice. Untracked directories are collapsed: status prints the directory, not the files in it. --untracked-files=all lists every file, and --untracked-files=no skips the scan, which is the expensive part in a large working tree. Second, status writes. By default it refreshes the cached file information in the index and writes the index back, taking a lock while it does.

beats.text: The manual's advice for background tools is git --no-optional-locks status. Third, status is local: a line such as "Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'" compares with the last fetched state, not with the server.

beats.text: Two pictures now. The textbook's analogy for the working tree: a workbench in front of a parts cabinet. The cabinet, the object database, holds labelled parts that never change. The bench is where you assemble and modify. Git can lay any stored version out on the bench again, but shavings and half-built parts that never went into the cabinet exist only on the bench.

beats.text: It breaks in two places. Git doesn't watch the bench. It looks only when a command asks. And the bench may hold things the cabinet has never seen, untracked files, which Git will list but doesn't protect.

beats.text: For status: a warehouse audit with three clipboards. What the last signed inventory says: HEAD. What the next inventory will say: the index. And what is on the shelves: the working tree. Status reads out the differences between neighbouring clipboards. It breaks because the middle clipboard isn't a list of differences. It's a complete inventory, and status computes the differences each time you ask.

It's a complete inventory, and status computes the differences each time you ask.

beats.text: Three boxes. Content moves right with add and commit, and back left with restore. Read the captions under the boxes: the right box holds every committed snapshot, the middle box one proposed snapshot, and the left box has no history and no second copy.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: Taking a clean git status to mean "the directory equals the commit". Root cause: ignored files are present and hidden; git status --ignored lists them.
beats.tele: Taking a clean `git status` to mean "the directory equals the commit". Root cause: ignored files are present and hidden; `git status --ignored` lists them.

beats.text: Thinking "tracked" means "committed". Root cause: tracked means "has an index entry"; a path becomes tracked at git add.
beats.tele: Thinking "tracked" means "committed". Root cause: tracked means "has an index entry"; a path becomes tracked at `git add`.

beats.text: Reading a path listed twice as a contradiction. Root cause: status makes two comparisons, and a file staged and then edited again differs in both.
beats.tele: Reading a path listed twice as a contradiction. Root cause: status makes two comparisons, and a file staged and then edited again differs in both.

beats.text: Parsing the long or short format in a script. Root cause: those formats follow user configuration and may change; --porcelain is the stable one, with -z for unusual file names.
beats.tele: Parsing the long or short format in a script. Root cause: those formats follow user configuration and may change; `--porcelain` is the stable one, with `-z` for unusual file names.

beats.text: Using git diff --exit-code to prove that a build left the tree clean. Root cause: it performs comparison two only, so a generator that created a new, untracked file passes unnoticed.
beats.tele: Using `git diff --exit-code` to prove that a build left the tree clean. Root cause: it performs comparison two only, so a generator that created a new, untracked file passes unnoticed.

beats.text: Now, out of the lab. A CI job has to prove that the build left the tree clean: generated code is committed, and the formatter changed nothing. The job should test git status --porcelain for empty output. git diff --exit-code isn't enough, for the reason you now know: it covers the index against the working tree and nothing else, so a generator that wrote a new, untracked file passes.
